content.description: **Alfred Hitchcock** invented modern suspense: give the audience information the characters do not have. In *Psycho*, *Vertigo* and *Rear Window*, he plays with where we look.

hero.hook: Real suspense does not surprise you: it lets you see the bomb under the table.

blocks.text: **Alfred Hitchcock** (1899-1980) was nicknamed the “master of suspense.” Across more than fifty films, he turned the thriller into an art of manipulation. *Psycho*, *Vertigo*, *Rear Window*: every time, the camera does much more than tell a story. It plays on our nerves.
His favorite subject is not crime. It is looking itself: guilt, obsession, voyeurism. Hitchcock films the viewer as much as the characters.

In **1966**, Hitchcock explained his method to [[François Truffaut]], a French critic turned filmmaker. **Surprise**, he said, is a bomb that goes off with no warning: a short shock. **Suspense** is showing the bomb to the audience while the characters know nothing about it. The tension lasts. We become accomplices, and powerless.

blocks.caption: Hitchcock: one face, one silhouette, a global brand of fear

blocks.text: To push the plot forward, he often used a [[MacGuffin]]: an object or a secret that drives the characters, but whose exact nature hardly matters. What counts is the chase.
This gap in information is his grammar. The moment we know more than the hero, we start to fear for him.

In **1948**, with *Rope*, Hitchcock faked one continuous [[sequence shot]]: the film looks as if it were shot in a single take. Reels lasted only ten minutes, so he hid the cuts behind a back or a dark piece of furniture. The effect is suffocating: we stay locked in with the murderers.

blocks.caption: Vertigo: dizziness filmed as a distortion of space

blocks.text: In **1958**, for *Vertigo*, he invented the [[Dolly Zoom]]: the camera pulls back while the lens zooms in, or the reverse. Space warps. We no longer see the vertigo. We feel it.

In *Rear Window* (**1954**), a photographer with a broken leg spies on his neighbors. He is the double of the viewer sitting in the dark. Hitchcock builds the scene on the [[point-of-view shot]]: we see exactly what the hero sees, nothing else.

That identification is moral as much as visual. We hunt for clues, but we also share the guilt of watching what is none of our business. Hitchcock mixes thriller and [[psychoanalysis]]: buried fears, forbidden desires, double identities.

Hitchcock turned his own name into a brand, right down to his television series *Alfred Hitchcock Presents*. For *Psycho*, he banned latecomers from the theater: keeping the secret became an event. His work with the composer [[Bernard Herrmann]] tied music to [[editing]] to speed up the pulse of the audience.
Hitchcock codified modern suspense: inform the viewer, steer their eye, and turn fear into controlled pleasure. Decades later, the thriller still owes him its grammar.

Bernard Herrmann.explanation: Iconic composer whose Music defined the atmosphere of Hitchcock's films, notably through the tense use of strings in Psycho.

Dolly Zoom.explanation: An effect of spatial distortion achieved by combining a zoom in and a camera dolly back (or vice versa).

François Truffaut.explanation: French filmmaker whose interviews with Hitchcock helped theorize the master's work and have him recognized as an auteur.

MacGuffin.explanation: Hitchcock's term for the object that all characters pursue (the suitcase, the secret plans) but whose content has no importance for the viewer. What matters is the desire it arouses and the narrative dynamics it generates.

Subjective camera.explanation: Technique where the camera adopts the point of view of a character, making the viewer experience exactly what they see. In Vertigo, Scottie's vertigo is transmitted by a zoom-out/dolly-in technique invented for the film.

Subjective camera (point of view shot).explanation: Technique where the camera adopts the point of view of a character, making the viewer experience exactly what they see. In Vertigo, Scottie's vertigo is transmitted by a zoom-out/dolly-in technique invented for the film.

The MacGuffin.explanation: Hitchcock's term for the object that all characters pursue (the suitcase, the secret plans) but whose content has no importance for the viewer. What matters is the desire it arouses and the narrative dynamics it generates.

editing.explanation: The assembly of a film's shots. Hitchcock used it to manipulate time and suggest actions without showing them explicitly.

point of view shot.explanation: Technique where the camera adopts the point of view of a character, making the viewer experience exactly what they see. In Vertigo, Scottie's vertigo is transmitted by a zoom-out/dolly-in technique invented for the film.

point-of-view shot.explanation: Technique where the camera adopts the point of view of a character, making the viewer experience exactly what they see. In Vertigo, Scottie's vertigo is transmitted by a zoom-out/dolly-in technique invented for the film.

psychoanalysis.explanation: A discipline exploring the unconscious, integrated by Hitchcock into his thrillers to deepen the psychological motivation of his characters.

sequence shot.explanation: A film sequence composed of a single, continuous shot, without any visible editing cuts.
